channel.title: California Uzbek — Latest
channel.description: Independent analysis · Central Asia & world geopolitics

item.title: Switzerland to return a further $252.5m from Gulnara Karimova's assets
item.description: The second tranche under a 2022 agreement; the first returned $87m. The money flows through the UN-backed Ishonch-2030 fund for children's health and education.

item.title: A $5 billion 'Aerocity' to be built next to New Tashkent airport
item.description: President Shavkat Mirziyoyev announced an 800-hectare development of logistics, e-commerce, hotels and housing; the master plan is due by July 2027.

item.title: Pentagon spent $81.5m holding migrants at Guantanamo — for just 849 people
item.description: A Defense Department Inspector General report found the base, prepared for tens of thousands, held only 849 migrants in total and never more than 399 at once.

item.title: 20-year-old Javokhir Sindarov is fighting for the world chess crown
item.description: The Uzbek grandmaster faces reigning champion Gukesh Dommaraju in Geneva — the youngest world championship match in history; winning needs 7.5 points over 14 games.

item.title: Uzbekistan's consulate in Mazar-i-Sharif to become a Consulate General
item.description: Under a presidential decree, the new status takes effect on 1 December; the decision aims to expand trade, transport-logistics and economic cooperation.

item.title: How US college admissions work: SAT/ACT, the Common App and the application process
item.description: Admission to a US undergraduate program is a step-by-step process: standardized tests (SAT or ACT), a single application (the Common App), an essay, letters of recommendation and application deadlines. This guide explains the process for immigrant and diaspora families — based only on verified facts, not as advice. Exact rules and deadlines differ by college and change every year, so always check the college's official page.

item.title: The '.uz' domain and the arrival of the internet in Uzbekistan (1995–2002)
item.description: In the early years of independence Uzbekistan began building its own digital identity: on 29 April 1995 the national '.uz' domain was delegated by IANA, the first internet connections appeared in the mid-1990s, and in 1999 the state placed the single international gateway in the hands of UzPAK. In 2002 that monopoly was eased and UZINFOCOM was created. The article relies only on dates confirmed by two or more reliable sources.

item.title: The Uzbek diaspora in France: a small, young community centered on Paris
item.description: The Uzbek community in France is small, relatively new and concentrated mainly around Paris. Because French statistics do not record ethnicity, the exact number of Uzbeks is not officially known. This article relies only on verified facts: from the 1929 Paris émigré press to today's restaurants and cultural organizations. No unverifiable figures or claims are presented.

item.title: Uzbekistan releases a 20-billion-token Uzbek corpus free to AI companies
item.description: The Ministry of Digital Technologies published Uzbek's national language corpus in open access; it was provided free to developers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Alibaba.

item.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec's ban on religious symbols
item.description: The Supreme Court kept the 2019 secularism law (Bill 21) in force; only the requirement that legislators uncover their faces was struck down unanimously.

item.title: EDB to provide up to $60m to Uzbek railways via Islamic financing
item.description: The Eurasian Development Bank will finance the purchase of 2,683 rail tank cars through a Shariah-compliant commodity Murabaha structure, for transporting petroleum products.

item.title: AfD leader Alice Weidel calls Islam 'Sharia', rejecting Le Pen's view
item.description: The AfD co-leader claimed on a Die Welt podcast that Islam and Sharia cannot be separated and dismissed France's Marine Le Pen's view that Islam is compatible with the Republic; Politico reported.

item.title: Mirziyoyev visits new AI-equipped road centre; $20bn in private investment sought
item.description: A scientific and practical centre of the Committee for Automobile Roads opened in Tashkent; special vehicles use AI to inspect roads and traffic.

item.title: Rights and obligations of a green card holder: what a US permanent resident should know
item.description: A green card (Permanent Resident Card) holder is a US lawful permanent resident (LPR). This article explains the rights and obligations of HOLDING the card, not of getting it: taxes, reporting an address change, travel abroad and maintaining status, and the path to citizenship. Based only on verified official information; this is not legal advice. Fees, timelines and rules change — always check uscis.gov.

item.title: How a power of attorney and an advance healthcare directive work in the United States
item.description: A power of attorney (POA) is a legal document that gives one person authority to make decisions about your money, property or affairs. An advance directive sets out your treatment wishes, or names a decision-maker, for when you can no longer decide for yourself. The rules vary from state to state in the US.

item.title: The Uzbek lodge and migration along the Hajj road: Central Asians' Ottoman tekkes (18th–20th centuries)
item.description: Long before the Soviet era, the Hajj was for Central Asians a long journey through Istanbul, Jerusalem, Damascus, Mecca and Medina. Along that road a network of tekkes — lodges for Uzbek, Bukharan and Kashgari pilgrims — took shape. The most famous is the 'Uzbeks' Lodge' in Üsküdar, Istanbul.

item.title: When a baby is born in Islam: adhan, tahnik, naming, aqiqah and circumcision
item.description: Islam has several recommended practices when a baby is born: reciting the adhan in the ear, tahnik, naming on the seventh day, aqiqah (a sacrifice), shaving the head and giving its weight in silver as charity, and circumcision. The ruling and emphasis differ between the schools of law. This article presents only verified facts and issues no religious ruling.

item.title: US Thanksgiving dinner costs rise: $58.63 for 10 people
item.description: The American Farm Bureau Federation says the dinner is up 6% and turkey 10%. A separate figure cited by Al Jazeera puts turkey up 26%.

item.title: Palestinian journalist killed in Gaza, Mariam Dagga, wins Rory Peck prize
item.description: Palestinian freelance journalist Mariam Dagga (33) won the prestigious Rory Peck prize posthumously. She was killed in an August 2025 strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.

item.title: Trial of Islamic State propagandist Émilie König opens in France
item.description: Émilie König, 41, faces up to 30 years at a Paris special court on a charge of “criminal association with a terrorist organisation.”

item.title: Hong Kong courts Uzbek tourists with combined Hong Kong–China packages
item.description: The Hong Kong Tourism Board came to the Tashkent fair for the first time; 7.6 million Uzbeks travelled abroad in 2025. A 30-day visa-free regime is still under discussion.

item.title: Uzbekistan and Afghanistan: the UN '6+2' group and the Tashkent Declaration (1996–2001)
item.description: In the first decade of independence, Uzbekistan's southern neighbor Afghanistan was engulfed in civil war. Tashkent did not recognize the Taliban government, closed the Friendship Bridge, and worked for a settlement within the UN-sponsored '6+2' group. In July 1999 the 'Declaration on Fundamental Principles for a Peaceful Settlement of the Conflict in Afghanistan' was adopted in Tashkent.

item.title: Growing hurdles haunt India’s interfaith couples
item.description: The Special Marriage Act’s 30-day public notice and anti-conversion laws expose Hindu–Muslim couples to threats from families and vigilantes.

item.title: Report: more than a third of Muslim students experience Islamophobia at UK universities
item.description: The Fosis 'Belonging in Question' report surveyed 715 students at 63 institutions. 38% had experienced Islamophobia, and 68% did not feel able to report it.

item.title: Israeli Heritage Minister Amichai Eliyahu calls Palestinians and Muslims 'camel riders' and 'barbarians'
item.description: The minister used the slurs during a speech in the Knesset on 24 November, in a debate on crime in Arab society in Israel.

item.title: The four Sunni schools of Islamic law: Hanafi, Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali — where they differ
item.description: Sunni Islam has four main schools of jurisprudence (madhhabs): Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. They agree on creed and fundamentals and differ mainly on secondary (furu') rulings. Uzbekistan and Central Asia follow predominantly the Hanafi school.

item.title: The Uzbek diaspora in the United Kingdom: a small but emerging community
item.description: The Uzbek community in the United Kingdom is a small, young diaspora based mainly in London. According to the 2021 UK Census, 3,810 people born in Uzbekistan were recorded in England and Wales. This article sets out the community's formation — from mid-20th-century Turkestani émigrés to the post-1991 stream of students, professionals and asylum seekers — on the basis of sources.

item.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, at the centre of the deportation battle, leaves the US for Spain
item.description: The Salvadoran man left the United States voluntarily. He had been mistakenly deported in 2025 and later returned under a Supreme Court ruling.

item.title: Diplomatic relations between Uzbekistan and India (1991–1996): the first years
item.description: India was among the early countries to recognise Uzbekistan's independence; the protocol establishing diplomatic relations between the two states was signed in Tashkent on 18 March 1992. This history article sets out the exact dates, first ambassadors, high-level visits of the 1990s, and the centuries-old historical and cultural backdrop, drawing on India's Ministry of External Affairs, the Embassy of India in Tashkent, and Uzbekistan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

item.title: Selective Service registration in the US: a guide for immigrant families
item.description: Almost all men aged 18–25 living in the US — citizens, green-card holders, refugees, asylees, and many undocumented men too — must register with the Selective Service within 30 days of turning 18. There is currently no active draft — this is only a standby list. Who must register, who is exempt, how to register, and the consequences of not registering. Based on sss.gov and USCIS — not legal advice.
